**Please note that this analysis comes from Wood Mackenzie’s new Metals & Mining Corporate Tool which includes over 2,600 assets, and 1,200 companies across 94 regimes.** **If you have any further questions please contact –** **sheona.griffiths@woodmac.com** # Glenstrata: King of the Miners? ## Executive Summary The European Commission has now given backing to Glencore’s $31bn (£19.5bn) bid to take over metals and mining firm Xstrata. The new company (“Glenstrata”) will have a market capitalization of about $70 billion and become the world's largest zinc miner, ferrochrome producer and thermal-coal exporter. By the end of the decade, it could become the world's biggest copper miner. However there are still a few more hurdles that Glenstrata will have to jump before the deal becomes official. Focusing on their metals & mining assets, namely: coal, iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, nickel, aluminium, and gold; Wood Mackenzie looks at how this new entity will dominate global supply of these commodities, the cost competitiveness of these assets, their project pipeline, and potential risks within each commodity. The Glenstrata deal, which still needs approval from several antitrust regulators, is the biggest merger and acquisition deal so far this year. Both companies have a good track record of acquisitions, and with their combined cashflow, this could mark the start of an aggressive acquisition period for the metals and mining sector. Although it would occur at a difficult time for the industry as companies adjust to the economic reality of lower prices and a decline in demand from fast-growing emerging economies. Glenstrata – King of the Miners? ## Background Glencore and Xstrata proposed a merger of equals in 2011, but the deal has been revised several times to appease the Xstrata shareholders. The deal has also seen the departure of Xstrata’s CEO and Chairman. Glencore’s business includes logistics and spans the whole commodity spectrum, from soft commodities such as corn, to hard commodities such as copper. Whilst Xstrata’s business is Tier 1 metals and mining assets. There is little synergy expected from the deal, but better vertical integration and risk diversification in some respect to some commodities. Coal

The first hurdle Glenstrata will need to comply with is the European Union’s condition that Glencore must scrap an exclusive deal with Nyrstar, the world's largest zinc metal producer, and sell its 7.8% stake in the firm. This requirement aims to ensure that the European zinc metal market is preserved.

The next hurdle for Glenstrata is to clear antitrust regulators in China, which is expected to rule by year-end; and gain approval in South Africa. Both firms already sell commodities in China and as they plan to increase market share in China, they must obtain clearance before the deal can proceed. #### **Corporate Cost Position in 2012** Xstrata is the largest producer of zinc in concentrate in the world with interests in a number of large long-established mines located in Australia, Canada and Peru - including Mount Isa, McArthur River, Antamina, Brunswick, Kidd and Perseverance. It also holds a majority stake in the Bracemac-Mcleod project in Canada, which is scheduled to enter production in Q1 2013. Xstrata’s zinc mine production will be impacted by the closure of Brunswick and Perseverance in 2013 with the loss of 370kt/a, plus an expected temporary 24% drop in zinc output at Antamina during 2013. Replacement tonnage will be sourced initially from expansion projects at existing mines, Xstrata’s 50%-owned Bracemac-Mcleod (65kt/a Zn) in 2013, Metals and Mining Corporate Tool - December 2012 Page 3 of 18 Glenstrata – King of the Miners? plus potential new mine capacity from Pallas Green (160kt/a Zn) and Hackett River projects (150kt/a Zn) later this decade. Xstrata has also acted to extend the mine life and expand capacity at existing assets. In March 2010 the company announced a A$133M project to expand the Black Star open pit mine at Mount Isa which would add four years of production through to 2016. Xstrata also announced in October 2010 a A$274M expansion of Mt Isa’s George Fisher mine to 4.5Mtpa ore by 2013. Mt Isa is expected to increase zinc production by around 130kt/a between 2013 and 2015, as high grade production from Lady Loretta comes online and George Fisher expands. Extensive reserves and resources at Mt Isa are likely to sustain production well past 2030. During 2011, Xstrata announced the successful feasibility study results for a major expansion of McArthur River from 2.5Mt/a ore to 5Mt/a ore, as well as extending mine life by six years to 2033. In 2012, the company announced that rather than produce additional bulk concentrate to be treated mainly in Albion leach circuits at Nordenham and San Juan de Nieva, it would produce a zinc concentrate suitable for treatment at conventional electrolytic smelters, as opposed to supplying a bulk concentrate to Imperial Smelting process (ISF) smelters as in the previous

plans. Contained metal production is expected to rise from 200kt/a to 380kt/a zinc from 2014. Xstrata assets currently produce just over 1Mt/a of zinc in concentrate and the net result of the above closures and expansions of operating and highly probable (Base Case) mines will see this level sustained to 2016. Beyond 2016, the closure of Kidd (2018) and gradual grade reductions at a number of operations may result in a fall in production, although there is potential to raise output through the commissioning of new Possible projects such as Pallas Green (160kt/a), Hackett River (150kt/a) and Errington-Vermillion (46kt/a) projects. In contrast to Xstrata, Glencore controls a large number of mine assets held by Kazzinc in Kazakhstan, Blackthorn Resources in Burkina Faso, Rosh Pinah in Namibia, Los Quenales in Peru and Sinchi Wayra in Bolivia and Argentina. Being the fifth largest producer, output from these assets currently totals over 500kt/a, averaging approximately 60kt/a per asset, which is just over a third of the average size of assets held by Xstrata. The Kazzinc mines are integrated with the company’s own smelters. The Ridder and Shaimerden mines are in the top quartile of the cost curve, whilst Zyranavosk has a more competitive position in the second quartile. Production from these mines currently totals approximately 250kt/a. The Perkoa project in Burkina Faso commenced production in November 2012, after Glencore acquired a 50.1% share in the project for $72M in 2009. Glencore also owns a majority share in Rosh Pinah mine in Namibia which has been in operation since 1969, with current reserves sufficient for a mine life to 2019. Glencore’s Los Quenales assets in Peru include Iscaycruz zinc mine and Yauliyacu, a significant silver producer with extensive resources. Despite being on the 54th percentile of zinc mine costs, the former was placed on care and maintenance in 2009 due to weak market conditions. In Bolivia and Argentina, Sinchi Wayra operates four main mining operations producing predominantly zinc with some lead and most of these mines benefit from significant silver by-product credits. Strike action has been an issue at some of these mines in recent years, as is opposition by local communities. Opposition to Sinchi Wayra operating the main section of Colquiri mine was a significant factor in the removal of the operating license and nationalization of the mine in June 2012. #### **Corporate Cost Position in 2012** Xstrata is

the largest lead miner in world, with production of around 240kt lead expected in 2012. Mined lead output is a co-product (~30% of net revenue) of zinc production at Mount Isa and is a by-product (<20% of net revenue) at McArthur River, Antamina and Brunswick. Being largely dependent on zinc production at these operations, future production will be driven by the expansion plans at the previously discussed zinc mines. Brunswick mine is scheduled to close in March 2013. Lead is also a by-product (<25% of net revenue) at the zinc mines owned by Glencore, with the exception of Aguilar, where lead is a co-product at just under 40% of net revenue. The company is currently the ninth largest mine producer of lead, expected to produce just over 80kt in 2012. With lead principally being a by-product of zinc production, future lead concentrate output is also largely a factor of zinc production, as discussed earlier. #### **Cost Position in 2017** #### **Corporate Cost Position in 2012** The McArthur River mine (MRM) in Australia has a production capability of 425kt/a bulk lead-zinc concentrate grading around 47% Zn and 9% Pb (200kt/a Zn and 43kt/a Pb) from ore milled of 2.5Mt/a. The elevated lead content of this concentrate makes it suitable only for treatment by the Imperial Smelting process (ISF). The ISF smelting sector has been in decline for the last two decades with only eight plants now operating – four in China, two in Japan, one in Poland, and one in India. However only five of these will be able to take McArthur River bulk, as the Shaoguan smelter in China is no longer allowed to treat imported concentrate following a pollution incident in 2010, and the Harima smelter has just been converted to treat secondary raw materials only. Worldwide ISF capacity of 410kt/a Zn and 185kt/a Pb is Metals and Mining Corporate Tool - December 2012 Page 6 of 18 Glenstrata – King of the Miners? more than enough to accommodate McArthur River’s output but it is a sector that is under pressure from rising costs, reduced profitability and, in China, made vulnerable following a number of pollution incidents involving thallium and lead emissions. Xstrata, of course, has been well aware of the fragile nature of its off-take market for McArthur River bulk concentrate and has been testing the use of the Albion atmospheric direct leach process at its plants located in Germany and Spain as a route to eliminate this market risk and clear the way for a major expansion of the mine. In a

press release on 7th August, Xstrata stated it will not adopt the Albion process but instead use advanced processing technology on site at MRM to produce a separate zinc concentrate from the bulk concentrate. No details of the process have been released but we speculate that it could be a selective leach of the galena (PbS) that would produce a leadrich leach residue whilst preserving zinc in the sulphide form for sale as a concentrate to the wider electrolytic smelter market. There are a number of solvents, ferric chloride, ferric sulphate, fluorboric acid and ferric fluosilicate for example, that can selectively leach galena but the use of any of these processes would be novel and carry technical risk. Alternatively, and perhaps more realistically, the process could be a modification to the conventional froth flotation process. One such example that has been successful elsewhere is a short-retention conditioning with sulphuric acid that alters the surface of the galena to lead sulphate allowing this to be depressed to the flotation tails leaving the zinc as sulphide to be differentially floated. Whatever the process adopted, it must at the very least be able to reduce the lead content of today’s bulk concentrate from 9-11% Pb to 2-3% Pb to allow treatment of the new zinc concentrate at conventional electrolytic smelters. ## Copper ### **Mined Copper Supply** Over the next decade, Xstrata’s copper mine production could potentially increase from 787kt/a to 2.4Mt/a, a 200% increase, while Glencore’s could potentially increase from 270kt to 527kt, a 100% increase, during the same period. A combined company could potentially produce 7% of global mine copper by 2022. No imminent sale or synergy of copper assets is expected as both companies’ copper assets are well diversified geographically. #### **Mined Copper Supply** 100%

#### **Cost Position in 2017** Metals and Mining Corporate Tool - December 2012 Page 7 of 18 Glenstrata – King of the Miners? #### **Corporate Cost Position in 2012** In the past, Glencore has successfully dealt with governments to develop mines in countries with high political and social risks and this experience can be applied to Xstrata’s projects which are currently delayed due to these very issues, such as Tampakan in the Philippines. Also, the merger can breathe fresh air into the Frieda River project in Papua New Guinea. While Xstrata is looking to sell the Frieda Project for around $2Bn, Glencore’s expertise in dealing with such projects might lead to reconsideration if the merger proceeds. Glencore’s copper projects are mainly Brownfield assets (such as KOV expansion in D.R. Congo), whil

e Xstrata’s main copper projects are Greenfield assets (such as Tampakan in Philippines, Frieda River in PNG and El Pachon in Argentina). The combined company will be expected to have a lower overall project completion risk than Xstrata’s standalone Greenfield projects. ### **Blister & Cathode Supply** #### **Blister Copper Supply** 100%

#### **Cost Position in 2017** The merger of Glencore and Xstrata is not expected to significantly affect their contribution to the copper blister production and refining sector. Four of the five currently operating smelters are located in countries where the proposed Glenstrata has a financial interest in the mines supplying the smelters. This strongly indicates that the future of these smelters will depend on the future of the mines. As stated earlier, the closure of Mount Isa has already been announced. Of the remaining three smelters only Mufulira can be classified as a low cost smelter, mainly due to its historically low labour costs. This smelter is gradually being expanded to meet increasing local concentrate availability and it is expected to reach a concentrate treatment capacity of ~850kt/a by the end of the decade. PASAR is the only true Custom smelter to be operated by Glenstrata and has recently been restarted following a catastrophic fire which closed the smelter for 6 months. There have been unsubstantiated reports that the capacity of the smelter and refinery at PASAR could be doubled but this would not significantly affect Glenstrata’s contribution to global capacity as it would serve to little more than replace the capacity lost by the closure of the Mount Isa smelter. #### **Cost Position in 2017 (energy adjusted)** The addition of Xstrat

a's coal portfolio expands Glencore's direct coal presence beyond Colombia and South Africa, with assets in Australia and Canada. The merger extends Glenstrata's position as the largest thermal coal exporter globally in 2012. We estimate Glenstrata will export 84 million tonnes of thermal coal in 2012, rising to 115 million tonnes in 2017. We expect Glenstrata's share of global thermal coal production to remain between 11-12% over this time period. A significant risk to achieving our forecast is the approval and development of the large-scale Wandoan project, with the decision to proceed recently delayed to early 2013. Under our base case, Wandoan would contribute 22 million tonnes to annual exports, however there is potential upside, with the possibility of scaling the mine upwards of 80 Mtpa. Glencore's only direct exposure to metallurgical coal exists through its Springlake mine in South Africa, with only 0.2 Mtpa exports. Xstrata will contribute significantly, with low-cost, metallurgical coal exports from Australia and Canada, which we estimate rising from 13.2 million tonnes in 2012 to 19.2 million tonnes in 2017. We expect Glenstrata's share of global metallurgical coal production to increase slightly over this time period from approximately 6-7%. The largest metallurgical coal mine owned by Xstrata is Oaky North in Australia, which exports approximately 5.5 Mtpa, of which Xstrata's share is 55%, or approximately 3 Mtpa. #### **Nickel Operations Cost Position in 2017** Includes unfunded projects

> Xstrata currently operates the integrated nickel operations in the Sudbury Basin, Canada, with the smelter fed by mine production from Nickel Rim South, Fraser (including Fraser Morgan) and Raglan. In addition, concentrate is sourced from its Sinclair mine in Australia as well as third party and other secondary feeds. Matte from Sudbury is refined in Norway at the Kristiansand refinery which also processes matte from the BCL smelter in Botswana as well as other third Metals and Mining Corporate Tool - December 2012 Page 12 of 18 Glenstrata – King of the Miners? party materials. Xstrata also produce ferronickel from its Falcondo operation in the Dominican Republic (85.26% owned) and is about to commence production at its 49% owned 60kt/a Ni Koniambo project in New Caledonia. Glencore currently operates the Murrin Murrin plant in Australia. In 2012, Xstrata is forecast to produce around 3.8% of global mined nickel (73kt) and 6% of global refined nickel (104kt) while Glencore is forecast to produce around 2% of global mined and refined nickel. The combined Glenstrata is forecast to produce around 6% of global mined production and 7% of global refined nickel on an equity basis. In the near to medium term the major potential growth project in terms of mined nickel production will be through the development of the Kabanga mine in Tanzania. This is undoubtedly one of the best, if not the best, undeveloped nickel sulphide resources in the world. This is a 50/50 joint venture with Barrick, and although as yet not committed to development, we fully anticipate a staged development initially to produce around 10kt Ni/a in concentrate increasing to over 40kt Ni/a in concentrate in a second stage. Total capital costs are estimated at around $420M for stage 1 with an additional $550M for stage 2. In addition, the company is evaluating an energy conversion project for Falcondo which would enable it to return to full capacity of 30kt Ni/a from the current 15kt Ni/a. ## Gold ### **Mined Gold Supply** #### **Gold Supply** 100%

#### **Cost Position in 2017** Metals and Mining Corporate Tool - December 2012 Page 13 of 18 Glenstrata – King of the Miners? #### **Corporate Cost Position in 2012** Glenstrata currently has six operations producing gold, with the Vasilkovskoye mine in Kazakhstan being the only primary gold mine. In 2012, Vasilkovskoye accounted for just over 40% of combined Glencore and Xstrata production, with the next biggest contributor being the Alumbrera mine. Due to the scale of their operations, in 2012 Xstrata and Glencore ranked 37th and 44th respectively for attributable g

old production. However, combined gold output for Glenstrata makes it one of the top 20 global gold producers. As Vasilkovskoye is the only primary gold producer within the groups’ portfolio, it is a little out of sync with the other operations. Growth potential from current projects is limited with the groups’ principal projects (Tampakan and Frieda River) subject to uncertain start up dates. Additional information is provided in the copper section. #### **Cost Position in 2017** Xstrata and Glencore only have minimal interests in producing iron ore mines, but iron ore has been highlighted as a major strategic growth commodity for both companies. West Africa is the clear area of focus, with Xstrata holding 50% of the Zanaga project in the Republic of Congo. Xstrata also purchased Sphere Minerals in 2011, which added projects in Mauritania to its exploration portfolio. Glencore has iron ore exposure through sales off take agreements with London Mining, from the Marampa mine in Sierra Leone, and from Bellzone's Forecariah mine in Guinea, plus has a shareholding in Core Mining which is exploring the Avima deposit in Republic of Congo. The financial strength of a combined Glenstrata means it would be able to consider making larger M&A plays in the iron ore sector, potentially targeting established producers such as Fortescue Metals Group, in order to rapidly gain market share, rather than slower and riskier organic growth through the development of new projects. ## Aluminium ### **Bauxite Supply** Neither Glencore International or Xstrata have ownership interests in any bauxite mines. Glencore owns a 100% stake in the shuttered Columbia Falls smelter in Montana, USA, and 10% of the Ke’ao smelter in Shandong province in China. Columbia Falls ceased production in 2009 as a result of high power and low metal prices. Despite an improved power deal by the Bonneville Power Administration in 2011 of US$36.32/MWh for two years, with revision in 2014, Glencore does not plan to restart this smelter due to low metal prices. We do not include a restart of the smelter in our base case nor do we envisage that the Glencore/Xstrata merger will affect the dynamics of Glencore’s aluminium smelter holdings.
